strengths: An insightful empirical and statistical validation (using CCA and Pearson correlation) showing that the gap between high- and low-resolution features resides in a consistent, low-rank semantic direction in the embedding space.

The proposed Vector Panning Feature Alignment (VPFA) is a highly lightweight, post-hoc module that does not require modifying or retraining the backbone ReID model, ensuring high computational efficiency during deployment.
Excellent experimental results across multiple CR-ReID benchmarks, consistently outperforming more complex joint-training and super-resolution-based methods.
Comprehensive generalization and ablation studies, demonstrating the method's applicability across different backbones (CNN, ViT, DeiT) and its extension to visible-infrared and text-image ReID.
weaknesses: The training of VPFA depends on having paired HR-LR training samples. While synthetic downsampling makes this easy, acquiring aligned real-world HR-LR pairs for diverse conditions can be challenging in practical surveillance scenarios.

Since it acts as a post-hoc feature correction module, it relies entirely on the frozen backbone's capacity to preserve some identity-discriminative cues in low-resolution inputs. Extremely low-resolution queries where cues are completely lost cannot be resolved.

The simulation of low resolution primarily relies on standard synthetic downsampling (e.g., bicubic). The robustness of the learned 'resolution direction' under more realistic and complex image degradations, such as severe motion blur, compression noise, or varying camera sensor characteristics, remains less explored.

strengths: The paper introduces an insightful empirical observation: resolution variations in person ReID feature space converge to a stable, structured semantic direction once identity-specific differences are averaged out. This is thoroughly supported by statistical validation (using Canonical Correlation Analysis and Pearson correlation).

The proposed Vector Panning Feature Alignment (VPFA) is simple, highly efficient, and post-hoc. Working entirely in the feature space as a lightweight plugin, it avoids the high computational cost of image-space super-resolution or the complexity of joint training of ReID backbones, achieving extremely fast inference (over 4.4M samples/second).

The evaluation is highly extensive. The method is validated on standard synthetic benchmarks (MLR-Market, MLR-CUHK03, MLR-VIPeR) and a real-world benchmark (CAVIAR), achieving state-of-the-art results. The appendix demonstrates remarkable generalization of this concept across different backbones, and even across modalities (visible-to-infrared and text-to-image).

The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear figures, intuitive conceptual explanations (linking back to vector offsets in semantic word embeddings), and a rigorous ablation study that clarifies the design choices (e.g., residual connections and tanh gate).
weaknesses: The method is heavily reliant on the availability of paired LR-HR features during training to learn the panning offset. While synthetic downsampling makes generating paired data trivial, collecting aligned LR-HR sample pairs for real-world scenarios without synthetic degradation can be challenging.

The core components (the MLP architecture with LayerNorm, residual connection, tanh gate, and the MSE-equivalent Vector Panning Loss) are technically standard deep learning building blocks. The technical novelty lies in the application and empirical justification of this feature alignment direction rather than a new architectural or mathematical framework.

The paper primarily conducts its statistical analysis of the structured resolution direction on synthetically downsampled datasets (Market-1501). It remains somewhat unclear whether this directional consistency holds as strongly in highly complex, non-uniform real-world degradations (such as varying camera styles, lens blur, and compression artifacts).

strengths: Interesting and well-supported empirical finding: The paper demonstrates both qualitatively and statistically (via CCA and Pearson correlation) that HR-LR feature discrepancy aligns along a consistent, low-rank 'resolution direction' once identity-specific variation is averaged out.

Highly practical and lightweight post-hoc design: Unlike typical cross-resolution ReID methods that require joint training or complex super-resolution modules, VPFA is a post-hoc MLP-based residual mapper. It introduces negligible computational overhead (4.4M samples/second inference) and requires no backbone retraining.

Comprehensive experimental validation: The method is validated on standard benchmarks (Market-1501, CUHK03, VIPeR, CAVIAR) and consistently improves over strong baselines. The appendix also demonstrates strong generalizability across different backbones (ViT, DeiT, CLIP-ReID, CNN) and modalities (visible-infrared, text-image ReID).
High-quality presentation: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with clear figures, rigorous statistical analysis, and thorough ablation studies.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat limited: The core architecture of VPFA is a standard multilayer perceptron (MLP) with a residual connection and a Tanh gate, trained using sample-level Mean Squared Error (MSE). While framing it as 'Vector Panning' and 'Vector Panning Loss' connects nicely to the motivation, the actual technical implementation is relatively straightforward and closely resembles standard feature adaptation/regression techniques.

Potential confounding factors in real-world pairing: For real-world datasets like CAVIAR, which lack perfectly aligned HR-LR pairs of the same instance (i.e., captured at the exact same moment), the paper does not fully explain how the pairwise samples are constructed. If pairs are constructed from different images of the same identity, the difference vector $z_{HR} - z_{LR}$ will inevitably contain other variations (e.g., pose, viewpoint, illumination), which might interfere with learning a pure resolution direction.

strengths: Intriguing and Well-Motivated Concept: Drawing an analogy to semantic vector offsets in word embeddings (e.g., King - Man + Woman = Queen) to identify a consistent 'resolution direction' in person ReID feature space is highly intuitive and novel.

Solid Empirical and Statistical Analysis: The authors do not just claim the existence of this direction; they thoroughly validate it using Cosine Similarity, Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA), and Pearson Correlation Analysis.

Outstanding Efficiency and Non-intrusiveness: Unlike prior methods that require complex super-resolution networks or end-to-end retraining, the proposed VPFA is a lightweight post-processing module. It is extremely fast and can be easily plugged into any frozen, pretrained ReID backbone.

Strong Experimental Performance: VPFA achieves state-of-the-art results on several CR-ReID benchmarks (MLR-Market-1501, MLR-CUHK03, MLR-VIPeR, CAVIAR) and demonstrates impressive cross-dataset and cross-modality generalization capabilities.
weaknesses: Limited Technical Novelty of the Architecture: The Vector Panning (VP) module is essentially a standard multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with residual connections trained via Mean Squared Error (MSE). While the motivation (vector panning) is interesting, the actual network design and loss function are very standard.

Dependence on Paired Training Data: The training of the VP module relies on having paired HR and LR features for the same identities to compute the prototype pairs. While easy to obtain via synthetic downsampling, this requirement might limit its applicability in scenarios where paired multi-resolution data is hard to obtain.

Robustness to Severe Degradation: Since the backbone is frozen, the method relies entirely on the backbone's ability to extract some identity-discriminative information from low-resolution images. If the resolution is extremely low and the backbone features collapse, a post-hoc MLP mapping might struggle to recover the identity. An evaluation of different backbones (e.g., CNN vs. Transformer) would also strengthen this study.

Minor Typos and Notation Inconsistencies: In Algorithm 1, Stage 2, step (c) mentions computing the loss using 'Eq. (2)', which is actually the formula for prototype definition, whereas it should refer to Eq. (6) or (8).

strengths: An elegant and intuitive perspective: Modeling cross-resolution discrepancy as a stable and consistent semantic shift direction in the feature space, drawing a creative analogy to word embeddings.

Solid statistical backing: The authors thoroughly validate their hypothesis using Cosine Similarity, Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA), and Pearson Correlation Analysis, showing that the resolution shift is structured rather than random noise.

High efficiency and ease of integration: Unlike prior works that rely on heavy super-resolution models or end-to-end retraining, VPFA operates as a lightweight, training-free post-processing plugin on top of a frozen backbone, leading to extreme inference speeds (over 4 million samples/second).

Outstanding experimental performance: The method consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on multiple synthetic and real-world benchmarks (such as CAVIAR, Market-1501, and CUHK03) by significant margins.
weaknesses: Ambiguity in training pair generation: In Section 5.2, the authors state that they compute identity-wise mean features to get the prototypes, but then mention sampling 5,000 pairs with 'identity-level shuffling'. Since the number of unique identity prototypes is limited (e.g., 751 on Market-1501), it is unclear how 5,000 pairs are constructed and what 'identity-level shuffling' mathematically entails.

Over-claiming of loss function novelty: The 'Vector Panning Loss (VPL)' is mathematically identical to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss. The geometric expansion in Eq. (7) is a basic property of the L2 distance via the law of cosines. Renaming a standard MSE loss to make it seem like a customized contribution is unnecessary.

Marginal generalization to other modalities: Although the authors claim strong cross-modal generalization in Appendix A.3, the performance improvements on visible-infrared ReID (+0.29% Rank-1 on RegDB v2i) are very marginal, indicating that the 'linear semantic direction' assumption is less robust for severe modality gaps.

strengths: The concept of representing resolution differences as consistent directional offsets in the feature space of frozen ReID models is simple, well-motivated, and backed by interesting statistical observations (such as CCA and Pearson correlation analyses).

The proposed Vector Panning Feature Alignment (VPFA) is lightweight and operates purely as a post-processing module. It requires no end-to-end retraining or architectural modification of the base ReID model, making it highly practical and efficient.

Extensive experiments on standard cross-resolution datasets show significant improvements over existing approaches, and the method demonstrates impressive generalization ability across different datasets, more challenging resolution ratios, and other modalities (visible-infrared and text-image ReID).
weaknesses: There is a contradiction regarding the need for identity (ID) labels. In Section 4.4, the authors state: 'Our training requires no ID labels and learns the resolution difference in the vector space.' However, Section 4.1 (Equation 2) and Algorithm 1 clearly describe grouping features by identity and computing mean-pooled prototype features to supervise the training. If grouping by identity is required, the training pipeline indeed relies on ID labels. This contradiction needs to be resolved.

The baseline comparisons in Table 3 may be somewhat unfair. The proposed method utilizes a very strong frozen backbone (TransReID) which already achieves high accuracy (90.3% Rank-1 on Market-1501, as shown in Table 4a). In contrast, many of the compared state-of-the-art methods in Table 3 were developed using older, less powerful backbones (like ResNet-50). To ensure a fair comparison, the authors should either evaluate the baseline methods using the same TransReID features or apply their VPFA module to a standard ResNet-50 backbone and compare it with the baselines.

The technical novelty of the Vector Panning (VP) module is somewhat limited. Training a small multilayer perceptron (MLP) with a residual connection and mean squared error (MSE) loss to map features from a source domain (LR) to a target domain (HR) is a standard feature translation/alignment technique in cross-domain learning.
